22. And Pharaoh charged. If he had not been transported with wrath and struck with blindness, he would have seen that the hand of God was against him; but when the reprobate are driven to madness by God, they persevere obstinately in their crimes; and not only so, but, like the deranged
“Vertiginosi, vel phrenetici.” — Lat. “Phrenetiques, ou demoniacles.” — Fr.
or frantic, they dash themselves with greater audacity against every obstacle. It is indeed commonly the case that cruelty, having once tasted innocent blood, becomes more thirsty for it; nay, in general, wicked men, as if excited by their course, grow hotter and hotter in crime, so that there is no end nor measure to their iniquity; but here, in this very desperate rage, we must perceive the vengeance of God, when he had given up the tyrant for the devil to destroy him, whilst we also remember his design both to try the patience of his people as well as to set forth his own goodness and power. The tyrant, finding that his snares and deceit availed nothing, now shakes off fear and flies to open violence, commanding the little ones to be torn from the breasts of their mothers and to be cast into the river. Lest there should be any lack of executioners, he gives this charge to all the Egyptians, whom he knew to be more than ready for the work. He spares the daughters, that, being enslaved and allotted to the Egyptians, they might produce slaves for their masters, whilst by them the races and names could not be preserved. Here it may be worth while to meditate on a comparison with our own times. Antichrist, with all his murderous agents, leaves in peace those who by their treacherous silence deny Christ, and are prepared to embrace as slaves every kind of impiety; neither does he exercise his cruelty, insatiable though it be, where he sees no manliness to exist; and he exults and triumphs, as if his end was gained, when he perceives any who had some courage in professing their faith fallen into effeminacy and cowardice. But how much better is it for us to die an hundred times, retaining our manly firmness in death, than to redeem our life for the base service of the devil.
EXODUS 2
Exodus 2:1-10
1. And there went a man of the house of Levi, and took to wife a daughter of Levi.
1. Abierat autem vir ex domo Levi, et acceperat filiam Levi.
2. And the woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.
2. Concepit autem mulier illa, et peperit filium; vidensque eum esse pulchrum, abscondit tribus mensibus.
3. And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river’s brink.
3. Et quia illum abscondere amplius non poterat, accepit ei arcam arundineam, et oblevit eam bitumine et pice, et reposuit in ca infantulum: exposuitque in carecto, juxta ripam fluminis.
4. And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him.
4. Stetit vero soror ejus eminus, ut cognosceret quid ei fieret.
5. And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river’s side: and when she saw the ark among the flag’s, she sent her maid to fetch it.
5. Porro descendit filia Pharaonis ut lavaret se in flumine: (deambulabant autem puellae ejus secus ripam fluminis:) et videns arculam in medio carecti misit ancillam suam quae illam tolleret.
6. And when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews’ children.
6. Quumque aperuisset, vidit ipsum infantulum: et ecce, puer flebat: et miserta illius dixit, Hic ex pueris Hebraeorum est.
7. Then said his sister to Pharaoh’s daughter, Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee?
7. Tunc dixit soror ejus ad fili am Pharaonis, Ibone ut vocem tibi mulierem nutricem ex Hebraeis quae tibi lactet infantulum?
8. And Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, Go. And the maid went and called the child’s mother.
8. Respondit ei filia Pharaonis, Vade. Profecta est igitur puella, et vocavit matrem pueri.
9. And Pharaoh’s daughter said unto her, Take this child away, and nurse it for me, and I will give thee thy wages. And the woman took the child, and nursed it.
9. Cui filia Pharaonis dixit, Tolle infantulum hunc, et lacta eum mihi, et ego dabo tibi mercedem. Tunc accepit mulier infantulum, et lactavit eum.
10. And the child grew, and she brought him unto Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water.
10. Crevit autem infantulus, et adduxit eum ad filiam Pharaonis, cui factus in filium, et vocavit nomen ejus Moseh, dicens, Quoniam ex aquis extraxi eum.

                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Therefore they did set over them task<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />masters <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Heb, <ns0:hi>masters of tribute,</ns0:hi> who were to exact from them the tribute required, which was both mony and labour, that their purses might be exhausted by the one, their strength by the other, and their spirits by both.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 15. 13.</ns0:note> to afflict <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>oppress,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>humble:</ns0:hi> to spend their strength by excessive labours, and so disenable them for the procreation of children.</ns0:note> them with their burdens: and they built for Pharaoh treasure-cities <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Where they laid the Kings money, or corn, which is reckoned among treasures, 2 <ns0:hi>Chro.</ns0:hi> 17. 12. and 32. 27. and wherein a great part of the riches of <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gypt</ns0:hi> consisted: for they had corn enough not onely for them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, but to sell to other countries: so that <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> was accounted the granary of the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Empire. Or, <ns0:hi>defenced cities,</ns0:hi> in which Garrisons were to be placed, which seems best to agree with the place and use of them. For they were in the borders of the land, and among the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> which appears concerning the one from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47. 11. (where the land in which they were placed is called <ns0:hi>Rameses,</ns0:hi> which in <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> consists of the same letters, with this <ns0:hi>Raamses,</ns0:hi> and seems to be so called then by anticipation from the City of that name now built in it) and may be reasonably presumed concerning the other: and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore it is most probable that they were built to keep the <ns0:hi>Isra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />elites</ns0:hi> in subjection and to hinder them from going out of the land.</ns0:note>, Pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thom and Raamses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>and as they afflicted them, so they multiplied,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplyed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Through Gods over-ruling providence and singular blessing, which God gave them purposely to hasten first their sorer af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fliction, and next, and by that means their glorious deliverance.</ns0:note>, and grew: and they were grieved <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">Through envy and fear.</ns0:note>, because of the children of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>cruelty,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>tyranny,</ns0:hi> with hard words and cruel usage, without mercy or mitigation<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> This God permitted for wise and just reasons. 1. as a punishment of their Idolatry, into which divers of them fell there, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 24. 14. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 20, 5, 7, 8. and 23. 8. 2. to wean them from the land of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> which other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise was a plentiful and desirable land, and to quicken their de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sires after <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi> 3. to prepare the way for Gods glorious works and <ns0:hi>Israels</ns0:hi> deliverance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 81. 6.</ns0:note> in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which was the basest and most laborious of all their ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vices.</ns0:note>: all their service wherein they made them serve, <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> with rigour.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And the king of Egypt spake to the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew midwives <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Such as not onely were employed about the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men, but were <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> themselves, not <ns0:hi>Egyptians,</ns0:hi> as some sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose, as may appear, 1. because they are expresly called not <ns0:hi>the midwives of the Hebrews,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>the Hebrew midwives.</ns0:hi> 2. the <ns0:hi>Egyptian</ns0:hi> midwives would not willingly employ their time and pains among the meanest and poorest of servants, as these were. And if they were sent in design by the King, he had lost his end, which was to cover his cruelty with cunning, and to perswade the people that their death was not from his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tention, but from the chances and dangers of child-bearing. 3. the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> women as they had doubtless midwives of their own, so they would never have admitted others. 4. they are said to <ns0:hi>fear God, ver.</ns0:hi> 17. 21.</ns0:note>, (of which the name of one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">You are not to think that these were the onely midwives to so many thousands of <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> women, but they were the most eminent among them, and it may be for their excellency in that profession called to the ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice of some <ns0:hi>Egyptian</ns0:hi> Ladies, and by them known to <ns0:hi>Pharaoh,</ns0:hi> who might therefore think by their own interest and by the promise of great rewards or by severe threatnings to oblige them to comply with his desires; and if he met with the desired success by them, he meant to proceed further and to engage the rest in like manner.</ns0:note> Puah.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">A seat used by women when ready to be delivered, conve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />niently framed for the midwives better discharge of her office.</ns0:note>, if it be a son, then ye shall kill him <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which it was not difficult for them to do, without much observation.</ns0:note>: but if it be a daughter, then she shall live <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either 1. because he feared not them, but the males onely; and some adde, that he was advised by one of their magicians, that a male-child should be born of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who should be a dreadful scourge to the <ns0:hi>Egyptians:</ns0:hi> or 2. they reserved them for their lust, or for service, or for the increase of their people and the raising of a fairer breed by them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 But the midwives feared God <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">More then the King, and therefore chose to obey God ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther than the King, their commands being contrary each to other.</ns0:note>, and did not as the King of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And the King of Egypt called for the mid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wives, and said unto them, Why have ye done this thing, and have saved the men-children alive?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the Hebrew women are not as the Egypti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />an women, for they are lively <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>vigorous</ns0:hi> and active in promoting the birth of their own children: or, like <ns0:hi>the beasts;</ns0:hi> which without any help of others bring forth their young. So the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word signifies, and so there is onely a defect of the particle of similitude, which is frequent, as I have noted before.</ns0:note>, and are deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered ere the midwives come in unto them <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This might be no lye, as many suppose, but a truth concerning many of them, and they do not affirm it to be so with all. And so it might be, either because their daily and excessive labours, joyned with the fears of the execution of the Kings command, whereof they seem to have gotten notice, did hasten their birth, as the same causes do commonly in other women, or because they, understanding their danger, would not send for the Midwives, but committed themselves to Gods providence and the care of some of their neighbours present with them. So here was nothing but truth, though they did not speak the whole truth, which they were not obliged to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Therefore <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Because they feared God, and spared the children, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 17 whereby they exposed themselves to the Kings displeasure, because they would not offend God by murdering the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren, which they might have done many times secretly, and therefore it was onely the fear of God, which restrained them from it.</ns0:note> God dealt well with the mid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) God greatly increased their Families both in chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren and posterity, and in wealth and other outward blessings. So this phrase is used <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 30. 30. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 25. 9. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 35. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 24. and 11. 38. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 127. 1. As <ns0:hi>houses</ns0:hi> are com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly put for families, so <ns0:hi>building</ns0:hi> is put for procreating of chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 16. 2. and 30. 3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying, Every son that is born, ye shall cast into the ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver, and every daughter ye shall save alive.</ns0:p>
